overview: origin: 15th century, probably compiled over a period of time during the later 3rd and 4th quarters of the century. England, probably Nottinghamshire. As Keiser (1999) has pointed out, the later copies of legal instruments in Item 28 make frequent reference to William Booth or Bothe (d. 1464), bishop of Coventry and Lichfield and later archbishop of York, and to others associated with him, notably members of the Worsley family. The appearance of the handwriting, and the possible dating of some of the watermarks to c. 1469 and c. 1477, tend to suggest that the manuscript may have been compiled over a period during the last quarter of the fifteenth century. The fact that Scribe C, who must have added item 27 at a date after 1483 (when the sweating sickness first appeared in England) also collaborated with Scribe A in the copying of item 6, lends substantial support to this suggestion. Items 26, 28 and 32 strongly suggest that the principal compiler of the manuscript (Scribe A) was a member or servant of the religious community at the collegiate church of Southwell, near Newark, in Nottinghamshire. In order to compile Item 28 he must have had access to the archive of William Booth, who often stayed at the archiepiscopal residence at Southwell, and in whose church he was buried in 1464. Item 26 indicates that the compiler was directly associated with a member of the Worsley family family, whose extensive connections with the community at Southwell (and with Booth) are evident in Item 28, and more generally in the Southwell visitation records of the later fifteenth century (printed by Leach (1891)). Regarding the contents of the manuscript, it is relevant to note that hawking and hunting were amongst the clerical misdemeanours identified during the visitations, and that there are also allusions to the fact that the community was troubled by plague from time to time. overview: origin: Third quarter of the 15th century. England. The manuscript was previously thought to be 'the earliest dated manuscript in humanistic script', copied at Oxford in 1441 by Thomas Clare, a monk of Bury St Edmunds. overview: origin: Copied between c. 1460-c. 1475. Probably compiled and copied by and for a priest of the chapel of the almonry of Christ Church Cathedral Priory in Canterbury. The music in this manuscript is attributed to a number of composers who were active in or had connections with Kent during the 1460s and 1470s. These include William Corbrond and John Nesbet who were Masters of the Lady Chapel choir at Canterbury Cathedral Priory (respectively 1470-1474; and 1474-1488). The music includes unusual blessings sung by the Boy Bishop at the feast of St Nicholas. According to Bowers (1982), the prominence of these blessings and the text Stans puer ad mensam point to an intended use at the chapel of the almonry of Christ Church, Canterbury: the almonry buildings housed a boarding school for eight boys who sang in the Lady Chapel choir, and participated in services in the almonry chapel. Here, they celebrated the Boy Bishop ceremonies annually. Bowers (1982) suggests that the manuscript may have been compiled and owned by one of the priests who was responsible for the upbringing of the boys. Charles (1962) Bower (1982)

In the only other two copies...the proem is omitted...and the name of Edward IV is substituted for that of Henry in lines 121 and 2880 (ff. 3v and 53r). 1458×c.1485. ?London. Copied by the so-called 'Hammond Scribe' between 1458 and c. 1485. The anonymous scribe is named after the Chaucer-scholar Eleanor Prescott Hammond (1866–1933) who first identified their hand in five manuscripts (see Hammond (1905) and Hammond (1929)). Subsequently, scholars have identified ten more manuscripts that were copied by the scribe (see Doyle (1959) and Mooney (2006)). Aside from this manuscript, their hand occurs in the following manuscripts: Cambridge, Trinity College, MS R.3.21 Cambridge, Trinity College, MS O.3.11 London, British Library, Add MS 29901 London, British Library, Add MS 34360 London, British Library, Arundel MS 59 London, British Library, Cotton MS Claudius A VIII London, British Library, Harley MS 78 London, British Library, Harley MS 372 London, British Library, Harley MS 2251 London, British Library, Harley MS 4999 London, British Library, Royal MS 17 D XV London, Royal College of Physicians, MS 388 Oxford, Bodleian Library, Rawlinson D.913 Worcester, Cathedral Library, MS F.172 As Mooney (2006) notes, the Hammond Scribe appears to have worked as a clerk in the household of Sir Thomas Cook, member of the Drapers' Company and Mayor of London in 1462-63, possibly under the supervision of his secretary John Vale. The latter's initials occur in a blue and red monograms(QJV for Quod John Vale) at the top of f. 2:1r. As Matheson (2006), I: pp. 65-93, argues, the scribe's spellings suggest that they originated from West Essex although they also used spelling forms occuring in sources from the Central Midlands and London. The dating for the scribe's work is based on two works that they copied into this manuscript: 1. A treatise on making and using scientific instruments that refers to a certain Multon (ff. 2:215r, 2:217r, 2:219r, 2:222r) with the date 1458 (f. 2:215r); 2. A medical recipe that is attributed to the physician Roger Necton who died in 1484. Although scholars have suggested that Multon may refer to the Hammond Scribe's name, it is also possible that he was the author or translator of the treatise (see Mooney (2006), I: pp. 55-63).

The main body of the manuscript, ff. 5r-320v was copied by , as indicated by his colophon on the monk Gregorios Gregorios, monk f. 320v, probably in the last quarter of the 16th century, as indicated by the combination of watermarks. This would be consistent with the style of script. The manuscript contains four successive sequences of quire signatures, while no items of content run across more than one such sequence and the same type of paper is shared only between the first two. This indicates that these portions were originally produced as separate entities. The last two quires, which lack signatures or the crosses marked at the beginning of most of the other quires, whose content is similarly distinct and which were written in a different ink from the preceding quires, probably constitute another such entity. Two portions also begin with prayers of invocation in the margin, suggesting the beginning of a new piece of work (ff. 117r and 261r). However, the fact that all of the four sections with signatures, and the first quire and part of the second quire at the end of the manuscript, were copied by the same scribe in the same format, and that he wrote a single colophon at the end of the last and briefest of the sections he copied, suggests that they were combined into a single volume at an early date. The presence of the colophon suggests that they were intended for this purpose before they left the scribe's possession. The first quire (ff. 1-4), shorter than the rest, not included in the first quire sequence, partly blank, and copied by different hands in a style suggesting a similar date to the work of Gregorios, was probably originally intended as endleaves. The last three folios of the last quire (ff. 321-323), following the colophon and copied by another hand of similar date, may have been originally left blank and intended for a similar purpose, before having additional content added at some point after the manuscript's completion.

The palaeography of the manuscript is typical of work produced in England and France in the second half of the twelfth century; a date of production in the early 13th century is not impossible on palaeographical grounds, but this manuscript would benefit from detailed palaeographical investigation in order to further discussions about its date and place of production.

The production of the original manuscript must be dated after 518, the earliest possible date for the composition of the treatise of Severus against Julian of Halikarnassos, one of the texts featured in the catena. On the basis of the style of script, it has been dated variously from the from the 6th to the 8th centuries, but an 8th-century date is currently considered most likely. Its transformation into the present palimpsest can be dated to the second half of the 12th century, the period of activity of the scribe Neilos, who copied a dated manuscript in 1170 and two more in 1180. Since the latter two manuscripts were produced on Rhodes, it may well be that the upper text of this manuscript was also copied there. The watermark of the paper leaf suggests that these repair elements,whose text is in the same hand, were added and copied during the later 14th century. This is consistent with the style of the script.

The characteristics of the scripts suggest that the manuscript was produced during the latter three-quarters of the 11th century. The consistency of layout and style of ornament between the portions copied by the different hands suggests that they worked as part of a single production project, despite the use of a different ruling pattern on each scribe's quires. However, Hand A does appear to have replaced a lost or cancelled folio originally copied by Hand B (f. 1r). The transition from Hand B to Hand C (ff. 56v-57r), occurring in mid-word, might suggest that C worked later than B. However, the fact that each page of the last two folios of Hand B's work (ff. 55r-56v) is ruled and written with an extra line suggests that this scribe may have adjusted to squeeze in the right amount of text before the existing beginning of Hand C's work. Falivene identifies the scripts as belonging to the minuscule bouletée style prevalent during much of the 10th century. However, while features of this style are present on occasion, including pronounced knobs at the end of strokes, short ascenders and vertical ascenders on delta, their presence is far from ubiquitous. Other features including the expansion of circumflexes above breathings and the accentuation of short nomina sacra are indicative of a date no earlier than the mid-11th century.

overview: origin: Copied between c. 1520-c. 1540 London The collection contains two dated recipes: one recipe for curing the Sweating Sickness, entitled ffor the new agew called the new acqueynttance A, is dated to 1540/1 (f. o xxxijo Regni Regis H[enrici] octaui111v); another recipe, entitled A souereyn medysyn for to stoppe a laske other of man or Chylde, has the year 1520 written above it (f. 115r). The manuscript's recipes refer to a number of patients and medical practitioners from early 16th-century London: Mastres Roppyssleys medycyn and plaster (f. 103r) may refer to the wife of Thomas Ropysley who is named a citizen and surgeon of London in his will of 1504. But the Mastres Wallwyn the Awdytours wyff who is also associated with the recipe must be must be one of the three wives of William Walwyn of Kensington, auditor for the king and the duchy of Lancaster, who made his will in 1535 ). She could be his first wife Kew, The National Archives, PROB 11/27/88Alice, who had died and was buried in St Bartholomew’s Hospital in West Smithfield when William made his will; his second wife Katherine whose marriage seems to have ended with divorce; or his third wife Sibylla (Sible) who was still alive in 1535. The collection also contains a recipe for curing toothache that is said to have been proved good by Sir John Thurston knyȝt (f. 115v). It probably refers to John Thurston, knight, goldsmith and alderman of the City of London whose will was drawn up in 1520. This identification can be confirmed from a recipe for treating pain in the limbs (f. 156v) that is said to have been proved by three men: two knights named John Thurston and Thomas Exmew, and a priest of a church dedicated to St Peter named John Chaunterell (quod probatum fuit per dominum Johannum Thurston militem et per dominum Exmew Militem et per magistrem johannum chawnterell rectorem ecclesie sancti petri). While the first is the aforementioned John Thurston, the second probably is Thomas Exmewe, another goldsmith and alderman of London (1508–29), who was Sheriff of London in 1508 and Lord Mayor of London in 1517. The priest probably is the John Chaunterell who was rector of the church of St Peter in Westcheap from 1492 until his death in 1509. The manuscript's second part contains two recipes that are attributed to a doctor Bentley: a medycyn tawght by magister doctor Bentley doctor of physyke (f. 124r) and good Medycyn [...] gevyn by Doctor bentley (f. 124r). He probably was Thomas Bentley who became Bachelor of Medicine at the University of Oxford in 1516, and received the degree of Doctor of Medicine in 1518. He was soon chosen as physician to the Duke of Buckingham. In 1521, he was several times consulted by Henry VIII. In 1523, he was appointed Censor of the Royal College of Physicians, and its President four times between 1525 and 1530 (see C.H. Talbot and E.A. Hammond, .The Medical Practitioners in Medieval England: A Biographical Register (London: Wellcome Historical Library, 1965), p. 334 On the basis of the previous identifications, the Master Twysellton who is mentioned in a recipe (ffor the fflyxe a medycyn whiche is callyd M. Twyselltons) on f. 103v may refer to John Twisleton who was a goldsmith and alderman of the City and died in 1525.

First half of the 11th century, perhaps as early as the fourth quarter of the 10th century. England. As with the place of origin (for which, see below), there is no clear agreement about the date of origin of this manuscript. Neil Ker (1957) proposed the mid-11th century, which, in Pam Robinson's analysis, appears to be confirmed by the inclusion among the apostles in the litany of St Martial, bishop of Limoges, whose apostolate was proclaimed by the bishop of Limoges in 1029, placing the copying of the manuscript at some point after that date. However, more recent studies have increasingly pushed the date of origin back: Paul Binski and Patrick Zutshi (2011) to the first half of that century, and David Dumville (1991) to the early 11th century, and Michael Lapidge (1992) still further to not much later than 1000 but potentially as early as the fourth quarter of the 10th century (and more specifically 975-992, a period in which Germanus, formerly abbot of Winchcombe, and monks from that house were resident at Ramsey Abbey). There is no definitive evidence for the place of origin for this manuscript, however various theories have been advanced on the basis of art-historical or text-historical bases. The manuscript has commonly been attributed to in Winchcombe Abbey Winchcombe (Abbey : Gloucestershire, England)Gloucestershire, on the grounds that the name of St Kenelm is picked out in the litany in rubricated rustic capitals (f. 274v): Kenelm was the son of the abbey's founder, Coenwulf of Mercia, and both were buried there. However, Michael Lapidge has pointed out that other liturgical books of this period contain similar emphases in their commemorations but have no evident connection to Winchcombe: for example, Orléans, Bibliothèque municipale, MS 127, whose origin was English but otherwise remains uncertain; and the Metrical Calendar of Ramsey (Oxford, St John's College, MS 17) and the Ramsey Psalter / Oswald Psalter (), both of which are 'indisputably linked' with London, British Library, Harley MS 2904 in Ramsey Abbey Ramsey AbbeyCambridgeshire. Furthermore, the litany in MS Ff.1.23 contains saints that point to an East Anglian origin: Æthelthryth, Seaxburh/Sexburg and Eormenhild, each of whom was connected with Ely, and Tova, who was venerated at Thorney, all of whom are found in demonstrably East Anglian liturgies in other manuscripts (such as , from Crowland Abbey; and Oxford, Bodleian Library, MS Douce 296, from the Abbey of Bury St Edmunds). Wenburg (spelt 'ƿenburga' in this manuscript) is also included in Harley MS 2904. Other links with Ramsey arise from the inclusion of Breton saints Samson, Machu and Budoc - the last of whom occurs only in MS Ff.1.23 and the Metrical Calendar of Ramsey.Vatican, Biblioteca Apostolica, MS Reg. lat. 12 Both Dumville and Lapidge have pointed to the religious career of Germanus (d. c. 1013) - who moved between houses at Fleury, Westbury (Gloucestershire), Ramsey, Winchcombe, back to Fleury, and then as abbot of a new foundation at Cholsey (Oxfordshire) - as possible explanation for the particular combination of saints in the litany in this manuscript. It may be that monks transferred from Ramsey to Winchcombe, and returned to their place of origin in 975, retained some of their west-country liturgical identity while adopting some of that belonging to their place of exile. This may not mean, however, that the manuscript was copied at Ramsey. The exemplar for the Old English text in this manuscript is not identified or has not survived, but its closest relative is that found in the Vespasian Psalter (), which was at Canterbury by the later medieval period and presumably there when additions were made by Eadwig Basan in the early 11th century. Obligations owed by Germanus to Sigeric, archbishop of Canterbury, and his successor Ælfric, may have given rise to 'cultural affiliations' between Cholsey and Canterbury, leading Dumville to conclude that this manuscript (and another, London, British Library, Cotton MS Vespasian A.iCambridge, University Library, MS Kk.5.32) 'may have been written at Canterbury or Cholsey, but...belong palaeographically to the Canterbury orbit, as well as having textual and liturgical links with that city'. Michael Lapidge also considered Canterbury a possibility, specifically St Augustine's abbey, 'however, the evidence of palaeography squares poorly with that of liturgy', since the litany 'in no way reflects the liturgical use of that house, for it omits St Augustine of Canterbury from its list of confessors'. If it were written at St Augustine's, it must have made use without adaptation of an exemplar from elsewhere, but on the balance of evidence it seemed to Lapidge more likely that the manuscript was made during the seventeen-year period in which Germanus and his Winchcombe monks resided at Ramsey.

Second quarter of the 9th century (Rodgers), or 1st or 2nd third of the 9th century (Bischoff). France, probably at the Benedictine monastery of Saint-Denis. 'The presumption that the Moore Palladius was written at St.-Denis is confirmed by the script, which may be placed at an intermediate point in the spectrum extending from the script of certain St.-Denis MSS of the late ninth century to that of MSS written there under Abbot Fardulf (793-806)... One help in dating the MS is its consistent use of the 2-form for abbreviations of -ur. This new form had appeared at Corbie before the end of the eighth century, and it gradually supplanted the archaic ur-symbol, identical with that used elsewhere for -us. So important a centre as St.-Denis is unlikely to have been slow in adopting the new and eventually universal 2-symbol: the use of the archaic ur-symbol for -us (as well as for -ur) was already a feature of the Fardulfus type. According to Lindsay, the old use of the symbol was generally obsolete by 820, and we may with some confidence place the Palladius in the second quarter of the ninth century' (see Rodgers (1971)). Bischoff, by contrast, dates the manuscript to 'IX. Jh., 1./2. Drittel'. In his introduction to Palladius (1975), Rodgers states that the manuscript 'was written at St.-Denis in the first third of the ninth century', but in his description maintains the date of 'probably the second quarter of the 9th century'. Written in England, 1220s × 1240s. The quire may have originated at . Its contents appear to be a humorous response to the preceding material: Malmesbury AbbeyMalmesbury, Benedictine abbey of St Peter and St PaulSol meldunensis is from one Geoffrey to another concerning the works of an Alexander, and Prophetia Merlini opens here with a letter from a Geoffrey to an Alexander (f. 214r). The wide spacing between its lines invites the addition of glosses. Its parchment wrapper would have allowed it to be added loose to the rest of the volume.
